?%c*Ufjtmhvq.760,!3$.text: So how can Sonic manage to ignore player input in this project? Well, I modified this block, "Terrain Detection", a little. Now it uses an "L/R Input" variable, which is used to directly tell GSE how much force we want to add to the left or to the right. This variable is first set to a number based on the mere input of the left and right arrows, then it is modified by the Boost code.

The Homing Attack actually takes up two values, "HomingL" and "HomingR", because once the attack is triggered it's locked into place. The usage of two variants was specifically to make sure the Homing Attack doesn't switch directions abruptly.
Well, actually people call this an "Air Dash", but I call it a Homing Attack, 'kay?

`t{x!5J#f)y2w6_wL/QA.text: Okay, so here's the first script that triggers an attack. It activates the "QuickFall" move, better known as Stomp.

M[4~LR*q(G^ixT)S8e,1.text:
The QuickFall script is really basic. When the attack is being performed, as long as Sonic is in the air he'll be diving downwards with practically no X Velocity (speed in the X direction) and a Y Velocity (speed in the Y direction) of 30. The X and Y velocities are actually kinda "inverted" in Genesis Sonic Engine; you might expect this script to make him fly upwards, but that's actually not the case.
Anyway, if he hits the ground, he'll transfer into the "QuickFallEnd" Script, where he just sits there until you release the down arrow key.

So if you hold down the Z key while jumping, this variable increases. Hold it for 4 frames, and Sonic will do a Spin jump. Otherwise his "hop" is performed, which has half of the full jump height and does not Spin but is faster.
Slower Spin jumps is actually the only part of the base gameplay that was really modified, apart from obvious things like removal of Spin Dash and ground Spinning.
